# Within-population statistics





## Theme of this chapter

Now that we have a _slendr_ `model` encoded in a reproducible R script and a
simulated genomic data in the form of a tree sequence `ts`, how can we compute
population genetic statistics from this data?

Computing statistics requires a specification of _what_ should be computed and
_how_. For instance, which individuals should a computation be performed on? If
groups of multiple individuals are involved then how do we group them?

Exercises in this chapter will demonstrate these techniques using the most
fundamental concepts of population genomics, namely $N_e$, nucleotide diversity,
and allele frequency spectrum. Rather than delving into the mathematical
underpinning of these statistics, they will be used to provide a familiar
context to show how easy it is to gain insight into (sometimes unintuitive)
behavior of statistics in general through simulation-based exploration.

More concretely, the coding exercises will focus on the testing of a
hypothetical inference method (using a toy example of $N_e$ inference) using
simulation-based benchmarking across a parameter grid.







## Literature

**In case you find yourself with extra time for some background reading**, I
recommend the following two chapters from the absolutely brilliant,
freely-available textbook called [_"An Owner's Guide to the Human
Genome"_](https://web.stanford.edu/group/pritchardlab/HGbook.html). I don't
think there's  better companion resource on population genomics theory to what
I'm trying to do in this practical, simulation-based workbook.

- [Chapter 2.1, _"Genetic Drift: What happens to alleles over
time?"_](https://web.stanford.edu/group/pritchardlab/HGbook/Release-2023-09/HGBook-2023-09-chapters/HGBook-2023-09-23-ch2.1.pdf):
A beautiful and simple introduction to the concept of effective population size,
the effect of genetic drift and mutation on the amount genetic diversity in a
population, Wright-Fisher model, etc. (i.e, the core ideas we explore in this
chapter through population genomic simulations).

- [Chapter 2.2, _"More on genetic drift: The
coalescent."_](https://web.stanford.edu/group/pritchardlab/HGbook/Release-2023-09/HGBook-2023-09-chapters/HGBook-2023-09-23-ch2.2.pdf):
A slightly more technical (yet still very easy to digest) dive into the
coalescent theory background of the topics introduced in the previous chapter
(and, therefore, also to the simulation exercises in this chapter), including
discussion of the allele frequency spectrum (AFS).









## Preparation


Let's start with the following single-population model to be able to exclusively
focus on statistics without having to deal with complexities of demographic
modeling itself.

**Restart your R session (`Session -> Restart R`), then look through the code
below to understand what it does and save it as `slendr_statistics.R`. Run the
entire script and inspect the produced visualization to make sure your
understanding of this toy model was correct.**

```{r}
#| output: false
#| collapse: true
library(slendr)
init_env()

pop <- population("pop", time = 2001, N = 5000)

model <- compile_model(populations = pop, generation_time = 1, direction = "backward")

plot_model(model)

ts <- msprime(model, sequence_length = 10e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8)

samples <- ts_names(ts)
```












## Exercise 1: Adding mutations

When you typed `ts` in your R console earlier, you may have noticed a strange
thing --- although `msprime()` simulated genomic data, there are no mutations!
How can this be? Just take a look the tree-sequence summary below (specifically,
the "Mutations" field):

```{r}
ts
```

As we will see later, the magic of tree sequences allows us to compute any
population genetic statistic without mutations. That said, for comparing
simulated results to statistics computed by various third-party software outside
of R, having mutations is often useful. Here's how we can make that happen.

---

**Modify the `msprime(...)` command in your script `slendr_statistics.R` by
"piping" its output to `ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)` (remember the `%>%`
"pipe operator" introduced earlier). After you execute this new command and type
`ts` in the R console to inspect the summary, you should see that mutations have
been added. Verify that this is the case by typing `ts` in your R console.**
  
::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
#### Click to see the solution

Here's the general pattern of how we simulate genomic data with _slendr_
including mutations:
  
```{r}
ts <-
  msprime(model, sequence_length = 10e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8) %>%
  ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)
```

We can see that, indeed, the tree sequence now has `{r} ts$num_mutations`
mutations in it:
  
```{r}
ts
```

:::

Even though mutations are generally not needed, there's almost never any huge
downside to adding them, so I recommend you always use both `msprime()` and
`ts_mutate()` in your models in this workshop.








---







With that out of the way, let's proceed with computing population genetic
statistics using _slendr_ and _tskit_.









## Exercise 2: Within-group(s) statistics --- nucleotide diversity

The simplest possible computation we can do is to compute a statistic for a
single population. As an example, let's look at [nucleotide diversity (also
known as $\pi$)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nucleotide_diversity),
implemented by the _slendr_ function `ts_diversity()`.

---

If you **look at its help page under `?ts_diversity`**, you will see that it
accepts several arguments---for now let's focus on the first two, `ts =` (which
is obviously a tree-sequence object, such as the one produced by the `msprime()`
engine) and `sample_sets =`.

**Compute `ts_diversity()` on a single simulated individual, such as the
individual with the name "pop_1", by providing this name as the `sample_sets =`
argument of this function. Knowing that _slendr_ simulates diploids and knowing
the definition of [nucleotide
diversity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nucleotide_diversity), how would you
interpret the result that you get for this one individual from the perspective
of genomics?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
### Click to see the solution

The answer is that we get that individual's heterozygosity---the proportion of
their complete genome (composed of two chromosomes, because each individual is
diploid) carrying heterozygous sites:

```{r}
ts_diversity(ts, sample_sets = "pop_1")
```

<!-- ```{r} -->
<!-- sum((ts_genotypes(ts)[, c("pop_1_chr1", "pop_1_chr2")] %>% rowSums()) == 1) / ts$sequence_length -->
<!-- ``` -->

Note that this is the same thing as the following command:

```{r}
ts_diversity(ts, sample_sets = c("pop_1"))
```

This is because in R, a single value is the same thing as a vector of length one
(this might seem like a bit of curious R trivia but it's good to keep in mind):

```{r}
"single_value" == c("single_value")

length(c("single_value"))
length("single_value")
```

:::

---

**Now run the following three commands, one after the other. They look extremely
similar, right? Do they produce the same value? If not, based on the results you
get from each of those commands, can you deduce a general rule for how _slendr_
interprets what it gets in the `sample_sets =` argument?**

```{r}
#| output: false
ts_diversity(ts, sample_sets = c("pop_1", "pop_42"))
ts_diversity(ts, sample_sets = list(c("pop_1", "pop_42")))
ts_diversity(ts, sample_sets = list(pop_subset = c("pop_1", "pop_42")))
```

::: aside

**Note:** It turns out that patterns like these are very important for computing
any kind of tree-sequence statistic with _slendr_, so it very much pays off to
think about this, even though this looks trivial and nitpicky!

:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
### Click to see the solution

- The first command is supposed to demonstrate that specifying a plain vector of
names to a statistic computed within a group computes that statistic as if each
individual was "its own group". In this example, we get individual-based
heterozygosity for each of the two individuals separately (notice that the
"pop_1" value is the same you got in the previous task):

```{r}
ts_diversity(ts, sample_sets = c("pop_1", "pop_42"))
```

- The second command features the same vector of names, but wrapped in `list()`.
This is how you instruct _slendr_ to treat a given set of individuals as a
group---and in this case, compute a statistic for the group as a whole. In this
context, this command computes the nucleotide diversity within a group formed by
the given two individuals from the population "pop":

```{r}
ts_diversity(ts, sample_sets = list(c("pop_1", "pop_42")))
```

- Notice that in the result above, _slendr_ assigned our group of two
individuals a rather non-descriptive group name "set_1". Because these default
names can be confusing in more complex computations of more complex statistics,
you can optionally specify the name of your group by providing the set of
individuals as a named list instead (see the [R bootcamp
chapter](r-bootcamp.html) in case you need a refresher on named lists and
similar topics):

```{r}
# note that the group name "set_1" is now replaced by "pop_subset"
ts_diversity(ts, sample_sets = list(pop_subset = c("pop_1", "pop_42")))
```

:::


---

Of course, we can compute any statistic not only for one group of individuals,
but for multiple of them. What result such computation produces depends on
whether we're computing the so-called ["one-way
statistics"](https://tskit.dev/tskit/docs/stable/stats.html#sec-stats-sample-sets-one-way)
(computed within groups, like nucleotide diversity we started with here) or
["multi-way
statistics"](https://tskit.dev/tskit/docs/stable/stats.html#multi-way-methods)
(computed between groups, like $F_{ST}$). For now we'll stay with one-way
statistics.

**To make the "one-way" statistic concept clear, let's practice this. Instead of
computing `ts_diversity()` for a single group of individuals (like "pop_1" and
"pop_42" above), compute it on multiple subsets of individuals of increasing
samples sizes (let's say groups of 1, 2, 5, 10, 500 1000, and finally all
individuals in the population "pop"). Before you run this computation, do you
expect the same value of nucleotide diversity for each of those sample sizes?
Why, or why not?**

**Hint:** You can get a random subset of a larger set of elements using the
built-in R function `sample()`. Take a look at `?sample` manual page if you need
more help. If you need even more help, take a peek at the beginning of the
solution below (point 2. specifically). When you have a list of the different
subsets of individuals, you can provide it as the `sample_sets =` argument of
`ts_diversity()` again.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
### Click to see the solution

Let's first generate the subsets of different sizes. We have a number of
options:

1. We could do it "manually" like this:

```{r}
# first get all names of all individuals recorded in the tree sequence
# as a single vector stored in the variable named `all`
all <- ts_names(ts)

# then "manually" create all required subsets
subsets <- list(
  sample(all, 1),
  sample(all, 2),
  sample(all, 5),
  sample(all, 10),
  sample(all, 500),
  sample(all, 1000),
  all
)
```

2. Alternatively, we could do it more succinctly using this neat R trick:

```{r}
# first create a vector of the desired sizes of all subsets
sizes <- c(1, 2, 5, 10, 500, 1000, length(all))

# then iterate over those sizes, applying the sample() function to each
subsets <- lapply(sizes, sample, x = all)
names(subsets) <- sizes
```

Either way, both approaches create a list of vectors of appropriate lengths that
we need to solve this exercise.

---

Having created the lists of subsets of individuals from the population, we can
finally compute nucleotide diversity in each of those groups like this:

```{r}
ts_diversity(ts, sample_sets = subsets)
```

Not surprisingly, we don't see much difference. This is expected, because there
is only one true (unknown) value of nucleotide diversity of the entire
population. What changes when we compute this statistic on subsets of different
sizes is the stochastic noise due to random chance.

We'll see a bit more on how to control (and quantify) the noise in simulations a
little bit later.

:::










## Exercise 3: Parameter estimation --- $N_e$

In practical research, we often use various software to estimate some model
parameter of interest. In our context---again, to demonstrate the concept of
simulation-based analyses in a familiar context---let's look at a measure of the
population size called [effective population
size](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Effective_population_size), or $N_e$, as
this model parameter of interest we want to infer.

From a bit of [background theory of population
genetics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Effective_population_size#Empirical_measurements),
we know that we can obtain an estimate of $N_e$ from nucleotide diversity (which
we just computed). Specifically, neutral theory of molecular evolution posits
that an idealised diploid population will have the nucleotide diversity (usually
called $\theta$ in literature) equal to

$$\theta = 4 N_e \mu,$$

where $\mu$ is the mutation rate. Using simple algebra to rearrange this
equation, this gives us an estimate for $N_e$ which can be computed from
nucleotide diversity in the form of

$$N_e = \frac{\theta}{4 \mu}.$$

**In principle, this is an estimate which could be computed by some external
software (in a more complex real-world scenario). Let's build a simple
simulation-based analysis to determine how well does this estimator perform
under different scenarios.**

::: aside

**Note:** If you are familiar with population genetics, this exercise has all
sorts of obvious answers, but let's demonstrate how we can benchmark this
estimate using simulations, establishing a useful _slendr_ recipe which you will
be able to use in many other contexts on many other inference methods (some of
the more complex ones will be demonstrated later in this workshop).

:::
 
---

**In your script `slendr_statistics.R`, start by computing nucleotide diversity
across all individuals in your tree sequence taken together (instead of a small
subset) and store this result of `ts_diversity()` in a data frame `df`. Then,
use the equation above to estimate $N_e$ from nucleotide diversity, adding a new
column called `Ne_estimated` to this data frame with this value. Do you get a
somewhat reasonably looking result?**

**Hint:** Remember that you know the true $N_e$ in your model --- it's the `N`
value in your simulation script! That's the most powerful thing about
simulations --- they allow you to establish a ground truth and benchmark various
methods against this truth!

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
### Click to see the solution

Let's get the data frame with the value of diversity first:

```{r}
df <- ts_diversity(ts, list(all = ts_names(ts)))
df
```

Then add the inferred $N_e$ according to the equation above:

```{r}
df$Ne_estimated <- df$diversity / (4 * 1e-8)
df
```

We programmed the true $N_e$ in our model at
`{r} attr(pop, "history")[[1]]$N`,
so this estimate doesn't look bad at all!

:::

Of course, benchmarking any method based on a single simulation of a single
number doesn't make much sense in practice---so now let's now take things one
step forward.









## Exercise 4: Generalizing the simulation

**Suppose we need to evaluate how our hypothetical statistic of interest (in
this example, our estimator of $N_e$) behaves under different parameters,
different models, different bioinformatic processing, etc. This happens very
often in practical research, so how would we go about it using simulations?**

To do this, we could make a copy of our original script, modify it a bunch of
times, and re-run the modifications as needed, collecting the results in the
process. This works, but is almost always the wrong approach. The correct way to
do this is to generalize our code into a self-contained function.

To demonstrate, let's break this down into individual steps (in software
engineering, this process of modifying code and improving it is called
["refactoring"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Code_refactoring)).

---

**First, save your current script `slendr_statistics.R` as a new script called
`slendr_Ne_pi.R`. We'll be working on improvements in this new file** (the `pi`
comes from a shortcut name for nucleotide diversity in mathematical theory
$\pi$).

---

**In this new script `slendr_Ne_pi.R`, create a new R function called
`sim_constant`, which will accept a single argument `Ne_true`, and will "wrap
around" the following bits of code (most of which can be copy-pasted from the
original `slendr_statistics.R` you worked on so far in this chapter, with minor
modifications):**

1. **the code implementing our _slendr_ demographic `model`** (substituting the originally fixed `N` value for `Ne_true`, of course),

2. **the command simulating a `ts` object from the `model`**,

3. **the command creating the `df` data frame with nucleotide diversity,**

4. **the computation of `Ne_estimated` from nucleotide diversity,**

5. **addition of a `Ne_true` column to `df` and assigning it the `Ne_true`
argument given to your function.**

6. **returning this `df` object as the output of the function.**

**When you're done, all code which was doing the steps above in your original
script should be entirely replaced by this function.**

**Hint:** If you need help with creating a custom function, you can use the
following template which shows what should your script look like when you're
done. Additionally, you can get a refresher on programming custom functions by
skimming the [relevant section](r-bootcamp.html#exercise-10-functions) of the
_"R bootcamp"_ chapter.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
### Click to see the template

```{r}
#| eval: false
library(slendr)
init_env()

sim_constant <- function(Ne_true) {
  # add the bits of code doing steps 1.-5. inside this function

  # finally, return the df data frame like this (step 6.)
  return(df)
}
```

:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
### Click to see the solution

Here's how my entire `slendr_Ne_pi.R` looks like. As you can see, it's basically
the same exact code as the script `slendr_statistics.R` we started with, just
"wrapped" in the `function(Ne_true) { ... }` block.

```{r}
library(slendr)
init_env()

sim_constant <- function(Ne_true) {
  pop <- population("pop", time = 2001, N = Ne_true)
  
  model <- compile_model(populations = pop, generation_time = 1, direction = "backward")

  ts <-
    msprime(model, sequence_length = 10e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8) %>%
    ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)

  df <- ts_diversity(ts, list(all = ts_names(ts)))

  df$Ne_estimated <- df$diversity / (4 * 1e-8)

  df$Ne_true <- Ne_true
  
  df
}
```

:::

---

**To test your function, restart your R session (in the RStudio top menu go
`Session -> Restart R`), then run your entire script again. Then, evaluate your
function in the R console by running it for different values of $N_e$ (for
instance, type `sim_constant(100)`, `sim_constant(1234)`, `sim_constant(20000)`,
etc.). Each of your function calls should produce a data frame with the
appropriate value of diversity and the estimated $N_e$.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
### Click to see the solution

Here's what I get with my implementation of this function:

```{r}
sim_constant(Ne_true = 100)
sim_constant(Ne_true = 1234)
sim_constant(Ne_true = 20000)
```

Again, it looks like our estimator can---at least on this extremely trivial
underlying demographic model---infer the hidden $N_e$ quite well.

:::

---

Doing all this extra programming work might seem like unnecessary bother. In
fact, it looks like we've written _even more code_ to make this happen! But the
pay off comes later, I promise.

**Custom functions are absolutely critical for efficient, reproducible science.
They eliminate copy-pasted bug-prone code and make it much easier to explore
ideas, test parameters, and explore various models. In this workshop, I'll be
often forcing you to write custom functions---hopefully, by the end you will
appreciate why I did this.**










## Exercise 5: Simulations across parameter grids

Whenever we want to benchmark a statistic or understand its expected behavior
under different circumstances, we need to re-run a model many times, usually for
different model parameters (or even different models entirely).

**Imagine we want to repeat our inference on many different potential values of
true $N_e$**. What we could do is something like what you did while testing your
function earlier, running the variations of the simulation individually and
manually. But this isn't scalable, definitely not if we need to run the same
model across a huge number of parameter values (or even multiple sets of such
parameters).

In cases like this, **we can use a "looping" function, such as the very
convenient function `map_dfr()` from the package _purrr_**.

---

**Let's demonstrate how this technique works. You don't have to run any of this
code, just skim through this demonstration to get an idea how this works and
apply it later.**

Imagine a silly little function like this, which creates a data frame with a
given number and its square:

```{r}
# define a custom function
silly_fun <- function(x) {
  return(data.frame(value = x, squared = x * x))
}

# run it for the value of x = 10
silly_fun(10)
```

The way **you use `map_dfr` is by providing a list of values of our parameter of
interest and a name of some function**. In the case of our silly function, we
can use `map_dfr()` like this:

```{r}
library(purrr)

map_dfr(c(10, 100, 1234, 20000), silly_fun)
```

The name `map_dfr` stands for _"`map` a given function producing a `d`ata
`f`rame and then bind its `r`ows together"_, hence, `map_dfr`. When you look at
its output above, this is exactly what happened.

---

**In your script `slendr_Ne_pi.R`, use the same technique program an automated
simulation of $N_e$ inference across a grid of `Ne_true` values of `c(1000,
2000, 3000, 4000, 5000, 10000, 15000, 20000)`. Use the function `map_dfr()` to
do this in an efficient, automated way, thus obtaining a single data frame.
Then, visualize the results in this data frame as a scatterplot of columns
`Ne_true` against `Ne_estimated`.** You can use _ggplot2_, or base-R plotting,
whatever you find easier.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
### Click to see the solution

```{r}
library(ggplot2)
library(purrr)

Ne_grid <- c(1000, 1500, 2000, 2500, 3000, 4000, 5000, 10000, 15000, 20000)

df_constant <- map_dfr(Ne_grid, sim_constant)

ggplot(df_constant, aes(Ne_true, Ne_estimated)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, color = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  ggtitle("True Ne vs Ne estimated from nucleotide diversity (constant population size)")
```

:::

---


This toy exercise is a great example of how to use these kinds of simulations in
practice. Again, nucleotide diverisity-based $N_e$ estimation and its
benchmarking across a range of parameters is only an example for demonstration,
but this idea extends to many other settings:

- benchmarking of IBD accuracy across different gene-flow scenarios,

- validating  qpAdm inference results for various possible admixture graphs,

- testing the robustness of local ancestry inference methods (LAI) and admixture dating inference as a function of admixture times and proportions,

- understanding how PCA differs for different sample sizes from different populations,

... and many others.










## Exercise 6: Comparing multiple models

Let's make it a bit more interesting and more practically relevant. **Suppose we
want to see how robust our estimator is to the assumptions behind the underlying
demographic model (which is almost always uncertain to some degree, meaning that
our assumptions can be also uncertain!).**

In the previous exercise, we used nucleotide diversity to infer the $N_e$ of a
population under study (we used an equation, but it could be also external
software) and verified that it works very well for a model of a constant
population size.

But **what about population that experienced a resize event? How well does our
$N_e$ estimate work in such case?**

---

**In your script `slendr_Ne_pi.R`, make a copy of your function `sim_constant()`
and name that copy `sim_change()`. Make the following changes to this
function:**

1. **the population "pop" will start with fixed $N_e$ of 5000,**

2. **the population will experience a population resize (implemented by the
function `resize()`), which will set the size of the population to the value
given to the argument `Ne_true` at time 1000.**

**Then, use `map_dfr()` to run the new function `sim_change()` along the same
parameter grid as before, visualizing the results of `Ne_true` against
`Ne_estimated` again. How well does our diversity-based $N_e$ estimate perform
in such a demographic scenario? Is it robust to non-constant demographic
histories? If not, why?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
### Click to see the solution

Here's the solution---new function `sim_change()`, new simulation run against a
parameter grid, and a visualization of results:

```{r}
# new function to simulate population size change
sim_change <- function(Ne_true) {
  pop <-
    population("pop", time = 2001, N = 5000) %>%
    resize(N = Ne_true, time = 1000)
  
  model <- compile_model(populations = pop, generation_time = 1, direction = "backward")

  ts <-
    msprime(model, sequence_length = 10e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8) %>%
    ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)

  df <- ts_diversity(ts, list(all = ts_names(ts)))

  df$Ne_estimated <- df$diversity / (4 * 1e-8)

  df$Ne_true <- Ne_true
  
  df
}

# simulations across a parameter grid
Ne_grid <- c(1000, 1500, 2000, 2500, 3000, 4000, 5000, 10000, 15000, 20000)

df_change <- map_dfr(Ne_grid, sim_change)

# visualization of results
ggplot(df_change, aes(Ne_true, Ne_estimated)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(color = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  ggtitle("True Ne vs Ne estimated from nucleotide diversity (population size change)") +
  xlim(0, 20000) +
  ylim(0, 20000)
```

We can see that even a large population resize event doesn't change the observed
levels of nucleotide diversity that much. As a result, the $N_e$ based on the
population nucleotide diversity is very wrong---we consistently estimate it at
the level of 5000 (i.e., the size prior to the resize), regardless of the true
size of the population after the resize.

It's only very drastic bottlenecks that are picked up by our $N_e$ estimator,
and even in those cases we still severely overestimate the true $N_e$ after the
resize event.

:::








## Exercise 7: Expanding the parameter grid

Our hypothesis for how poorly the nucleotide diversity-based estimate of $N_e$
is doing under non-constant population size is that the resize event is very
recent. As a result, diversity hasn't yet reached an equilibrium value which
would be picked up by our $N_e$ estimator.

Let's test this hypothesis while, at the same time, showing how we can expand
the parameter grid simulations to include another parameter---this time the time
of the population size change in addition to the $N_e$ resize value.

---

**In your script `slendr_Ne_pi.R`, add a second argument to your function
`sim_change()` called `T_change`. Change the `resize()` command in your function
to use variable `T_change` instead of the fixed value of 1000, then add another
column called `T_change` to the data frame with the value of this argument
before the function returns the results again. Then, run four versions of the
`map_dfr()` command in the same way as before, except now in the form such as
`map_dfr(Ne_grid, sim_change, T_change = 100)`** (this will run `sim_change()`
for each of the `Ne_grid` values like before, while fixing the `T_change`
parameter to 100). **Do this for `T_change` of 1, 100, 1000, and 2000.**

**When you visualize the results for each of the four simulation batches, do you
see evidence supporting our hypothesis for why our $N_e$ estimator performs
poorly in sudden changes of $N_e$? And does the time since the resize change
have an effect on the estimator as we hypothesized?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
### Click to see the solution

Here's the solution.

First, the new function `sim_change()` which now has two parameters `Ne_true`
and `T_change`:

```{r}
sim_change <- function(Ne_true, T_change) {
  pop <-
    population("pop", time = 2001, N = 5000) %>%
    resize(N = Ne_true, time = T_change)
  
  model <- compile_model(populations = pop, generation_time = 1, direction = "backward")

  ts <-
    msprime(model, sequence_length = 10e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8) %>%
    ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)

  df <- ts_diversity(ts, list(all = ts_names(ts)))

  df$Ne_estimated <- df$diversity / (4 * 1e-8)

  df$Ne_true <- Ne_true
  df$T_change <- T_change
  
  df
}
```

A new simulation run against a parameter grid (I'm `rbind()`-ing all four
`map_dfr()` runs together because I want to use _ggplot2_ to visualize the
results in a tidy way with four panels:

```{r}
Ne_grid <- c(1000, 1500, 2000, 2500, 3000, 4000, 5000, 10000, 15000, 20000)

df_change <- rbind(
  map_dfr(Ne_grid, sim_change, T_change = 1),    # simulate size change 1 generation ago
  map_dfr(Ne_grid, sim_change, T_change = 100),  # simulate size change 100 generations ago
  map_dfr(Ne_grid, sim_change, T_change = 1000), # etc.
  map_dfr(Ne_grid, sim_change, T_change = 2000)
)
```

And finally, visualization of results:

```{r}
ggplot(df_change, aes(Ne_true, Ne_estimated)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(color = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  ggtitle("True Ne vs Ne estimated from nucleotide diversity (population size change)",
          subtitle = "Each panel indicates the time of the population size change") +
  xlim(0, 20000) +
  ylim(0, 20000) +
  facet_wrap(~ T_change)
```

Here's the same result, plotted in a single figure:

```{r}
#| message: false
library(dplyr)

df_change %>%
  mutate(T_change = factor(T_change)) %>% 
ggplot(aes(Ne_true, Ne_estimated, color = T_change, group = T_change)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth() +
  ggtitle("True Ne vs Ne estimated from nucleotide diversity (population size change)") +
  xlim(0, 20000)
```

We can see that, indeed, the older the population resize event, the more time
there's for the population to lose genetic variation (in case of a bottleneck),
or gain new variation (in case of population size increase---though we don't
really see the effect here), which means that the $N_e$ estimated based on the
$\theta = 4 N_e \mu$ nucleotide diversity parameter is going to be a little
closer to the true (unknown) population size.

Still, it's absolutely clear that non-constant demography can completely mislead
the $N_e$ estimator based on nucleotide diversity---this is a conclusion that is
actually quite relevant for real-world applications. For instance, we could have
very endangered species (with a very small $N_e$) which still maintains quite a
bit of nucleotide diversity!

:::

---

In conclusion, the problem with the nucleotide diversity is that it effectively
reduces the entirety of genetic variation in the population (which mutations
there are at which frequencies) into a single number. As a result, we lose a lot
of potentially very useful information about the population's demographic
history. When we try to estimate $N_e$ using this summary statistic, we can only
hope to infer a long-term $N_e$, but we won't be able to infer recent population
dynamics.

As we have seen, a single bottleneck doesn't cause nucleotide diversity to drop
significantly enough for us to pick up that this bottleneck even happened.







## Exercise 8: Real-world example

To put the simulation-based exploration above in a real-world context, let's
consider the case of estimating the $N_e$ of a present-day modern human
population.

**Take a look at the [Supplementary Table
1](https://www.nature.com/articles/nature18964#Sec10) published in this [hugely
influential paper](https://www.nature.com/articles/nature18964). Look up the
value of heterozygosity computed for the individual with the sample ID
"S_Czech-2" in the column called "samtools autosomal heterozygosity". What is
the $N_e$ value you can estimate from the heterozygosity observed in this
individual, if you assume autosomal human mutation rate $\mu$ of $1.3 × 10^{−8}$
per base pair, per generation (`1.3e-8` in R) and substitute the individual's
heterozygosity for the $\theta$ parameter?**

**Knowing what you've learned from your simulation benchmarking of this simple
$N_e$ estimator above, how does your inferred modern human $N_e$ fit in the
context of the fact that there are more than 8 billion people in the world right
now?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
### Click to see the solution

In the Excel sheet we see the following heterozygosity for this individual:

```{r}
theta <- 0.00085124
```

Using our $N_e$ equation, this gives us the estimate of $N_e$ like this:

```{r}
Ne <- theta / (4 * 1.3e-8)
Ne
```

We can see that this $N_e$ value is drastically lower compared to the billions
of people alive today. This reflects the fact that---although there are so many
of us alive today---human population for most of our history was very small,
which is why the $N_e$ that we estimated reflects a kind of average of
population sizes over the past few millions of years.

:::









## Bonus exercise: Allele frequency spectrum (AFS)

**Create a new script called `slendr_Ne_afs.R`. Copy-paste the following code
into that script. Note that this is the same exact model we started this chapter
with (except for the one line which selects only 20 individuals from all
individuals recorded in the tree sequence).**

```{r}
library(slendr)
init_env()

pop <- population("pop", time = 2001, N = 5000)
model <- compile_model(populations = pop, generation_time = 1, simulation_length = 1000)

ts <-
  msprime(model, sequence_length = 10e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8) %>%
  ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)

subset <- sample(ts_names(ts), 10)
```

---

Unlike nucleotide diversity which, as mentioned above, reduces the entire
genomic variation of a population into a single number, the [allele frequency
spectrum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allele_frequency_spectrum) carries
information about the distribution of the counts of mutations at each observable
frequency.

**Look at the `?ts_afs` help page to learn how the _slendr_ function `ts_afs()`
works. As you've seen, `ts_diversity()` (like the vast majority of _slendr_
statistical functions) produces a data frame. What data format does `ts_afs()`
produce? Compute the AFS from your simulated tree sequence `ts` on your `subset`
of individuals, then visualize it (with whatever means you know).**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
### Click to see the solution

As we can see, `ts_afs()` produces a plain R vector of integer numbers, each of
which represents the count of mutations observed at a given frequency --- the
count of singletons, the count of doubletons, etc.:

```{r}
afs <- ts_afs(ts, sample_sets = list(subset))
afs
```

This vector can be easily visualized with a base-R function `plot()`:

```{r}
plot(afs, type = "l", col = "lightblue", xlab = "allele frequency", ylab = "count")
```

:::

---

But does the AFS really carry more information about demographic changes?

**Write a new function in your script, called `sim_afs()`, which will again
accept a single argument `Ne_true` and implement the exact same demographic
model as you did in your function `sim_change()` (i.e., resize from the initial
`N` of 5000 to the given value of `Ne_true` at time 1000). In this function,
compute the `afs` vector from this model, then run it for a range of `Ne_grid`
values and visualize the individual AFS vectors produced for each of them. Does
AFS pick up signal even from such recent population size changes, unlike the
nucleotide diversity?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
### Click to see the solution

Here's a function which simulates an AFS for a demographic history given by the
`Ne_true` argument:

```{r}
library(ggplot2)
library(purrr)
library(dplyr)

library(slendr)
init_env()

sim_afs <- function(Ne_true) {
  pop <- population("pop", time = 2001, N = 5000) %>% resize(N = Ne_true, time = 1000)

  model <- compile_model(populations = pop, generation_time = 1, direction = "backward")

  ts <-
    msprime(model, sequence_length = 10e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8) %>%
    ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)

  subset <- sample(ts_names(ts), 10)
  
  afs <- ts_afs(ts, sample_sets = list(subset))
  
  # return the result not as a plain integer vector, but a proper data frame
  # annotated by the frequency bin number -- this makes visualization of
  # results later with ggplot2 much easier
  data.frame(
    Ne_true = Ne_true,
    frequency = 1:length(afs),
    count = afs
  )
}
```

We run the AFS simulation batch in the same way as we did before:

```{r}
df_afs <- map_dfr(Ne_grid, sim_afs)
```

And we visualize the individual AFS vectors, colored by their underlying assumed
$N_e$ after the demographic history change:

```{r}
ggplot(df_afs, aes(frequency, count, color = factor(Ne_true))) +
  geom_line() +
  ggtitle("AFS vector for different population size change models")
```

For easier comparison, here are the AFS result side-by-side with the
values of nucleotide diversity from the same demographic scenarios:

```{r}
#| echo: false
cowplot::plot_grid(
  ggplot(df_afs, aes(frequency, count, color = factor(Ne_true))) +
    geom_line() +
    ggtitle("AFS vector for different population size change models"),
  ggplot(dplyr::filter(df_change, T_change == 1000), aes(Ne_true, diversity)) +
    geom_point() +
    geom_smooth(color = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
    ggtitle("True Ne vs Ne estimated from nucleotide diversity (population size change)") +
    xlim(0, 20000) +
    facet_wrap(~ T_change),
  nrow = 2
)
```


This simulation indicates that AFS does, indeed, carry much more information
about population history, even for recent changes in population size, driven
largely by singletons! Therefore, at least for population expansions, AFS is
much more statistically powerful than nucleotide diversity. From population
genetic theory perspective this makes sense, because nucleotide diversity is
actually nothing but a summary of the AFS.

:::

---

For now we'll leave this topic be. We could go much deeper into this, but the
point of this chapter was to demonstrate how to compute within-population
statistics with _slendr_, how we can use manipulation of R lists and vectors to
instruct _slendr_ on how to compute a given statistic, and provide a set of
small examples of how population genomic simulations (even extremely simple
ones!) and a bit of data processing can be used to benchmark real-world
inference methods..

Towards the end of the workshop, you'll have the opportunity work through a
slightly more realistic case-study which will demonstrate how to do
simulation-based inference of $N_e$ in a fully automated way.







## Catching up

Here is a complete solution to the exercises in this section represented by a
single tidy reproducible R script:

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
### Click to see the entire script

For simplicity, this script only evaluates models when the size change happens
1000 generations ago (but it could be expanded, of course).

```{r}
#| output: false
#| collapse: true
# first we import a couple of packages ------------------------------------

library(ggplot2)
library(purrr)

library(slendr)
init_env()

# function which simulates a constant size model --------------------------

sim_constant <- function(Ne_true) {
  pop <- population("pop", time = 2001, N = Ne_true)
  
  model <- compile_model(populations = pop, generation_time = 1, direction = "backward")
  
  ts <-
    msprime(model, sequence_length = 10e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8) %>%
    ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)
  
  df <- ts_diversity(ts, list(all = ts_names(ts)))
  
  df$Ne_estimated <- df$diversity / (4 * 1e-8)
  
  df$Ne_true <- Ne_true
  
  df
}

# function which simulates a model of population size change --------------

sim_change <- function(Ne_true) {
  pop <- population("pop", time = 2001, N = 5000) %>% resize(N = Ne_true, time = 1000)
  
  model <- compile_model(populations = pop, generation_time = 1, direction = "backward")
  
  ts <-
    msprime(model, sequence_length = 10e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8) %>%
    ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)
  
  df <- ts_diversity(ts, list(all = ts_names(ts)))
  
  df$Ne_estimated <- df$diversity / (4 * 1e-8)
  
  df$Ne_true <- Ne_true
  
  df
}

# function which simulates the AFS from a size change model ---------------

sim_afs <- function(Ne_true) {
  pop <- population("pop", time = 2001, N = 5000) %>% resize(N = Ne_true, time = 1000)
  
  model <- compile_model(populations = pop, generation_time = 1, direction = "backward")
  
  ts <-
    msprime(model, sequence_length = 10e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8) %>%
    ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)
  
  subset <- sample(ts_names(ts), 10)
  
  afs <- ts_afs(ts, sample_sets = list(subset))
  
  # return the result not as a plain integer vector, but a proper data frame
  # annotated by the frequency bin number
  data.frame(
    Ne_true = Ne_true,
    frequency = 1:length(afs),
    count = afs
  )
}

# run simulations across a given grid -------------------------------------

# for the constant model, these values represent the constant Ne, for the size
# change model they represent the final Ne after the initial size of 5000

Ne_grid <- c(1000, 1500, 2000, 2500, 3000, 4000, 5000, 10000, 15000, 20000)

df_constant <- map_dfr(Ne_grid, sim_constant)
df_change <- map_dfr(Ne_grid, sim_change)
df_afs <- map_dfr(Ne_grid, sim_afs)

# visualize the results ---------------------------------------------------

# diversity in the constant size models
ggplot(df_constant, aes(Ne_true, Ne_estimated)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, color = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  ggtitle("True Ne vs Ne estimated from nucleotide diversity (constant population size)")

ggsave("constant_size_pi.pdf")

# diversity in the size change models
ggplot(df_change, aes(Ne_true, Ne_estimated)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(color = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  ggtitle("True Ne vs Ne estimated from nucleotide diversity (population size change)") +
  xlim(0, 20000) +
  ylim(0, 20000)

ggsave("changing_size_pi.pdf")

# AFS in the size change models
ggplot(df_afs, aes(frequency, count, color = factor(Ne_true))) +
  geom_line() +
  ggtitle("AFS vector for different population size change models")

ggsave("changing_size_afs.pdf")
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
unlink(c("constant_size_pi.pdf", "changing_size_pi.pdf", "changing_size_afs.pdf"))
```

:::
